2636.t: From Proto-Hellenic *skʰíd͏̌d͏̌ō, from Proto-Indo-European *skid-yé-ti, from *skeyd- (“to divide, split”).

2664.t: Beekes gives Proto-Hellenic *auhḗr (“morning mist”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewsér, from *h₂ews- (“dawn; east”). Cognate with αὔρα (aúrā) (< *h₂éwsreh₂), Latin aurōra.

2637.t: From Proto-Hellenic *twálos, from Proto-Indo-European *tuh₂-(e)l-o- ~ *tweh₂-(e)l-o-, from *tewh₂- (“to swell; to crowd; to be strong”).

2622.t: From Proto-Hellenic *prógʷlāmə. Equivalent to προβάλλω (probállō, “to throw before”) + -μα (-mă).

2650.t: First found from the Egyptiots Aretaios and Dioskurides, a borrowing from Coptic ⲭⲁⲕⲓ (khaki), ⲕⲁⲕⲉ (kake), ⲕⲉⲕⲉⲓ (kekei, “darkness”) from Egyptian kkw (“darkness”), acknowledging its providing shade in the desert, with a preformative analogical to ἄκανθα…

2695.t: Probably from Aeolian ζάλευκος (záleukos, “very white”) [with -α-!], from regular Attic δι⁽ά⁾-λευκός [with -ι-, -α-]

2644.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pʰlegō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to blaze, burn”). Cognates include Sanskrit भर्ग (bharga) and Latin flagrō.

2699.t: Uncertain. Beekes proposes a possible pre-form *Βακτήρ (*Baktḗr), which may relate to βάκτρον (báktron) in the same manner as ἀροτήρ (arotḗr) connects to ἄροτρον (árotron).

2606.t: From Proto-Indo-European *snḗh₁wr̥ (“band, sinew”). Cognate with Latin nervus, English sinew, Sanskrit स्नावन् (snā́van, “tendon, muscle, sinew”), Old Armenian նեարդ (neard), and Avestan 𐬯𐬥𐬁𐬎𐬎𐬀𐬭𐬆 (snāuuar^ə).

2662.t: Utimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂erk- (“to protect, guard, hold, contain”).

2634.t: From συντίθημι (sŭntĭ́thēmĭ, “to place or put together”).

2653.t: Perhaps from an earlier *ἀμυ-νϝ-ω (*amu-nw-ō), a thematicized nasal present verbal formation (a la κλίνω (klínō) and πλύνω (plúnō)) from a root ἀμυ- (amu-) which may also be found in ἀμεύομαι (ameúomai, “to surpass, outstrip”), though the semantics are…

2648.t: From Proto-Hellenic *agorā́, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂goréh₂, from *h₂ger- (“to gather”); equivalent to ἀγείρω (ăgeírō, “to gather”) + -α (-ā, abstract noun suffix). Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀀𐀒𐀨 (a-ko-ra).

2604.t: Traditionally derived from a Proto-Indo-European *mewHdʰ- (“to complain, be emotional about”), and compared with Latin maereō (“to mourn”). However, Beekes argues in favor of a Pre-Greek origin, based on the suffix -σος (-sos).

2641.t: From τεῖχος (teîkhos, “wall, fortification”) + -ίζω (-ĭ́zō, suffix used to form verbs from nouns, adjectives and other verbs).

2686.t: From ὁμόλογος (homólogos, “in agreement”), from ὁμός (homós, “same”) + λόγος (lógos, “reasoning”), + -έω (-éō, denominative verbal suffix).

2665.t: Appears to be a locative of a derivative of the root Proto-Indo-European *h₂er- (“to fit”). Compare ἀραρίσκω (ararískō), Old Armenian արդ (ard), Lithuanian arti, and Latin ars.

2608.t: As if from *νουθέτης (*nouthétēs), from νοῦς (noûs) + τίθημι (títhēmi) + -της (-tēs), + -έω (-éō).

2639.t: From a zero-grade of Proto-Indo-European *twer- (“to twirl, swirl”); see the related σαίρω (saírō, “to sweep”) for cognates.

2614.t: According to Beekes, the semantic field of architecture, as well as the presence of the element "-ινθ-", suggest a loan from Pre-Greek.

2605.t: Alteration of νάω (náō, “to flow”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)neh₂- (“to flow; to swim”).

2603.t: From Aramaic 𐡌𐡍𐡄 (mnh), from Akkadian 𒈠𒉡𒌑 (manû).

2600.t: Deverbative of μέριμνα (mérimna, “anxiety, concern”). Cognates include Latin memor and Sanskrit स्मरति (smarati, “to think, to recollect”)

2631.t: Beekes concludes that this may be Pre-Greek based on the derivations with π instead of β.

2629.t: Perhaps from an adjective *στρωμνός (*strōmnós, “spread”) -ή (-ḗ), itself from στρῶμα (strôma).

2652.t: From Proto-Indo-European *h₂meh₁- (“to reap, mow”). Cognate with English mow and Latin metō.

2689.t: From Proto-Indo-European *h₃rewH- (“to howl, roar”), albeit with initial long ὠ- (ō-) unexplained. Cognate with Latin rūmor, Latin rāvis, Latvian rûkt, Lithuanian rū́kti, and Sanskrit रव॑ (ráva).

2673.t: From ἐπι- (epi-, “epi-, on-”) + βιβάζω (bibázō, “to cause to mount, put on”).

2651.t: Due to its late attestation, probably borrowed from Aramaic אִמָּא (ʾimmā), rather than a native sound-symbolic nursery word similar to those found in a wide variety of languages, e.g.
